read.sections.0.heading.source: Bring the object and its history together
read.sections.0.heading.back: Bring the object and its history together

read.sections.0.text.source:
Throughout this course, artworks and buildings have connected material choices with people's lives in different societies. A comparison is an account of the similarities and differences that matter. A comparison between cultures explains more than where an object was made. It asks who made or supported a work, and how people used it. It also asks what the work meant in a particular setting, and how its meaning changed. Nations contain many communities, and communities also exchange ideas across borders. A clear explanation keeps these relationships visible. It also says what its sources can and cannot establish.

Return to the two objects from Lesson 16. One is a bronze Buddha from Thailand; the other is a terracotta architectural element from Java. Their photographs let us compare material, form and the surviving features visible in each image. They do not show an original full-body pose. Their collection records add information about place, period and type of object. The photographs and the records answer different questions. Using them together gives us more than either one alone.
read.sections.0.text.back:

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
In this course, art and buildings have shown how people lived. A comparison looks at how things are alike and how they are different. A good comparison asks more than where a thing was made. Who made it or paid for it? How did people use it? What did it mean, and how did that change? A country has many communities. Communities also share ideas across borders.

Look again at the two objects from Lesson 16. One is a bronze Buddha from Thailand. The other is a baked clay piece of a building from Java. The photos let us compare their material and shape. They do not show a whole body. The museum records tell us the place, the time and the kind of object. Photos and records answer different questions. Together they tell us more.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
In this course, art and buildings have shown how people lived. A comparison looks at how things are similar and how things are different. A good comparison asks more than where a thing was made. Who made it or paid for it? How did people use it? What did it mean, and how did that meaning change? A country has many communities. Communities also share ideas across borders.

Look again at the two objects from Lesson 16. One is a bronze Buddha statue from Thailand. The other is a piece of baked clay from a building from Java. The photos let us compare their material and shape. The photos do not show a complete body. The museum records tell us the place, time and type of the object. Photos and records answer different questions. Together, both tell us more.

read.sections.1.text.source:
The new cases in this course extend this approach. A Mughal album joined works and skills connected with several regions. An Ifugao landscape depends on links between land, houses and shared work. Two different pictures of Diponegoro's arrest connect artistic choices with colonial power and later national memory. Mexico's temporary arts show how a shared festival name can include different local practices. These examples give us questions for comparison. They do not give one feature to every member of a nation.

A short explanation might connect the Javanese work's architectural title with its surviving form. It would also admit that the record does not identify its original building. This is a worked example of careful reasoning. It does not need an invented temple name or an imagined scene. Uncertainty is something the evidence we have does not settle. A missing detail can stay a question.
read.sections.1.text.back:

Two different pictures of Diponegoro's arrest connect artistic choices with colonial power and later national memory. Temporary arts in Mexico show how one shared festival name can include different local practices. These examples give us questions for comparison. These examples do not give one feature to every member of a nation.

A short explanation might connect the Javanese work's architectural title with its remaining form. That explanation would also admit that the record does not identify its original building. This is an example of careful reasoning. This example does not need an invented temple name or an imagined scene. Uncertainty is something the evidence we have cannot decide. A missing detail can remain a question.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
Other lessons give us more questions. A Mughal album joined art and skills from many lands. An Ifugao landscape links land, houses and shared work. Two paintings of Diponegoro's arrest link art with colonial power and memory. In Mexico, one festival has many local forms. These lessons help us ask questions. They do not mean that all the people in a country are the same.

Here is a careful way to explain. The Javanese piece has a title that links it to a building. Its shape fits that. But the record does not name the building. So we should not make up a temple name. Uncertainty means something the evidence does not settle. A missing detail can stay a question.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
Other lessons give us more questions. A Mughal album combined art and skills from many places. An Ifugao landscape connects land, houses and shared work. Two paintings of Diponegoro's arrest connect art with colonial power and memory. In Mexico, one festival has many local forms. These lessons help us ask questions. These lessons do not mean all the people in a country are the same.

This is a careful way to explain. The piece from Java has a title that connects it with a building. Its shape fits that title. But the record does not name its building. So we should not make up a temple name. Uncertainty means something the evidence cannot decide. A missing detail can remain a question.

read.sections.2.text.source:
The same approach works for a building. An outside photograph may show shape and material. A dated conservation report can explain how it is looked after. The views of people who use a place can add knowledge about its continuing meaning. These sources do not have the same purpose. A report about a restoration may tell us little about every visitor's experience. Evidence is information that supports a claim, so choosing evidence means matching it to the question.

In 2022, the International Council of Museums (ICOM) wrote a definition of a museum. It names research, conservation, interpretation and public access as important parts of museum work, along with the participation of communities. These aims help explain why a collection is more than a room of attractive things. Objects can support learning about beliefs, skills, trade, institutions and change. They do this best when explanations recognise the people connected with them.

There is room for more than one interpretation, or explanation supported by evidence. Different historians might stress making, religious meaning, architecture or collecting. They still need to respect the evidence. A clear account does not rank whole cultures by beauty. It does not assume that the largest, oldest or most expensive work matters most. Instead, it explains the significance of a particular relationship: why it matters in a stated context. And it makes its reasoning clear to another reader.
read.sections.2.text.back:

The views of people who use a place can add knowledge about its continuing meaning. These sources do not have the same purpose. A report about a restoration may tell us little about every visitor's experience. Evidence is information that supports a claim, so choosing evidence means matching it to the question.

In 2022, the International Council of Museums (ICOM) wrote a definition of a museum. That definition names research, conservation, interpretation and public access as important parts of museum work, along with the participation of communities. These aims help explain why a collection is more than a room full of beautiful things. Objects can support learning about beliefs, skills, trade, institutions and change. Objects do this best when explanations recognise the people connected with them.

There is room for more than one interpretation, that is, an explanation supported by evidence. Different historians might emphasise making, religious meaning, architecture or collecting. They still need to respect the evidence. A clear account does not rank whole cultures by beauty. That account does not assume that the biggest, oldest or most expensive work is the most important. Instead, that account explains the significance of a particular relationship, that is, why that relationship matters in a stated context. And that account makes its reasoning clear to another reader.
read.sections.2.text.note: "significance" is "kepentingan" (importance); the loan "signifikan" exists but is formal.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
It works the same way for a building. A photo can show its shape and what it is made of. A dated report can tell how people care for it. The people who use a place can tell us what it means to them. Each source has its own job. Evidence is information that supports a claim. Pick the evidence that fits your question.

In 2022, ICOM, a world group for museums, said what a museum is. It said a museum studies, cares for and explains objects. It is open to the public, and communities take part. So a collection is more than a room of nice things. Objects can teach us about beliefs, skills, trade and change.

There can be more than one good interpretation. An interpretation is an explanation backed by evidence. Historians may look at different things. But they must stick to the evidence. A good account does not rank cultures by beauty. Big, old or costly does not mean it matters more. Significance means why something matters in a stated context. A good account makes its reasons clear to others.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
The same way suits a building. A photo can show its shape and its building material. A dated report can tell how people look after it. People who use a place can tell us what it means to them. Each source has its own job. Evidence is information that supports a claim. Choose the evidence that suits your question.

In 2022, ICOM, a worldwide group of museums, stated what a museum means. ICOM said a museum studies, cares for and explains objects. A museum is open to the public, and communities take part. So a collection is more than a room full of beautiful things. Objects can teach us about beliefs, skills, trade and change.

There can be more than one good interpretation. An interpretation is an explanation supported by evidence. Historians may look at different things. But they must hold to the evidence. A good account does not rank cultures by beauty. Big, old or expensive does not mean more important. Significance means why something is important in a stated context. A good account makes its reasons clear to other people.

write.prompt.source: In four short sentences, compare the two works. Use one thing you can see and one fact from a record. End with one question that is still not answered.
write.prompt.back: In four short sentences, compare the two works. Use one thing you can see and one fact from a record. End with one question that is still not answered.

write.example.source: Both works show the head of the Buddha. One difference is that the Thai head is made of bronze, but the piece from Java is made of baked clay. The record calls the Java piece an architectural element. So it was once part of a building. A question that remains is which building it came from. The museum record does not say.
write.example.back: Both works show the head of the Buddha. One difference is that the head from Thailand is made of bronze, but the piece from Java is made of baked clay. The record tells us that the piece from Java is an architectural element. So the piece was once part of a building. A question that remains is which building the piece came from. The museum record does not say.
